title: Natural law (CCC 1954–1960)
hookLine: a moral sense written in human reason, shared across cultures

cards: Two small children at a playground, on holiday, from two different countries. They share no language at all. They've been taking turns on the slide, and it's working.
Then one cuts in front. The other doesn't need a single word: hands on hips, a frown, a finger pointing back at the line. Everybody watching understands it at once: that's not fair.
Nobody taught them the same rulebook, the same religion, or any religion. And still each recognized the same wrong. Paul noticed something like this, writing to the Christians in Rome.

teach.b: The phrase is natural law. Not the laws of nature, like gravity: a moral law.

teach.h: A LIGHT OF UNDERSTANDING FROM GOD.
teach.b: The Catechism says it expresses the original moral sense that lets a person tell, by reason, good from evil, and truth from a lie.

It quotes Saint Thomas Aquinas: the natural law is the light of understanding placed in us by God, by which we know what we must do and what we must avoid. God gave this light, Thomas says, at creation. Why natural?
Not because animals follow it, but because reason, which declares it, belongs to human nature.
Paul, writing about people who never received the law of Moses, says that when they do by nature what the law asks, they show, in the Douay-Rheims, "the work of the law written in their hearts."

The natural law, the Catechism says, is present in the heart of each person, and it quotes the Roman writer Cicero: there is a true law, right reason, in agreement with nature, spread among all people.

How it's applied varies, and takes reflection, across places, times and circumstances. But the law itself is unchanging through history; even when it's denied, it can't be destroyed or erased from the human heart.
It always rises again. Last, an honest limit. Not everyone sees its precepts clearly and at once.
That's why, the Catechism says, people need grace and revelation too, so moral truth can be known easily, firmly and without error. Tomorrow picks up that word, grace.

how: Catholic moral teaching appeals to natural law when speaking with people of every faith or none, arguing from reason as well as from scripture.

games.q: a friend says, "if people don't share my religion, we have nothing to say to each other about right and wrong." what does the Catechism's natural law teaching suggest?
o: that's right; morality is only for believers.
there's common ground written in human reason.
everyone's sense of right and wrong is just personal taste.
games.why: the Catechism says the natural law is present in every heart and shared through reason, even as its application varies.

practice: Think of something people react to the same way across ages and backgrounds, someone cheated, a promise broken, a child treated cruelly, a stranger who stopped to help, and stay with it.
Notice whether you had to look it up, and whether it shows up anywhere in the body, or nowhere at all. If you pray, give thanks for that light; if you don't, let it be there a moment longer.

wordCard.voice: Natural law. The moral sense written in human reason, by which people tell good from evil: in the Catechism's words, a light of understanding placed in us by God. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: written in reason. Common ground can run deeper than a shared rulebook. See you tomorrow.
